title: Alcohols and carboxylic acids
categories: Ethanol oxidation and comparing the families

questions.prompt: What does one line in the structural formulas represent?
options: One covalent bond, a shared pair of electrons.
A double bond with two shared pairs.
questions.explanation: One line represents one shared electron pair; two lines represent a double bond.

questions.prompt: In CH₃, what does the subscript ₃ count?
options: Three hydrogen atoms attached to that carbon.
questions.explanation: A subscript applies to the element immediately before it: H₃ means three H atoms.

questions.prompt: What is the total molecular formula of CH₃–CH₂–OH?
questions.explanation: Count two C, 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 H, and one O.

questions.prompt: Which group identifies the simple alcohols studied here?
options: Any O and H anywhere in a molecule.
A bonded –OH on a saturated carbon, outside a carboxyl group.
questions.explanation: An alcohol hydroxyl is bonded within the molecule; the complete neighbouring structure matters.

questions.prompt: Which arrangement is the complete carboxyl group?
questions.explanation: The same carbon has a C=O double bond and a single bond to O–H.

questions.prompt: In the acid drawings, which atom joins both the upper O and lower OH branches?
questions.explanation: C is double-bonded to O above and single-bonded to OH below.

questions.prompt: How many bonds, counting a double bond as two, surround the carboxyl carbon?
questions.explanation: C=O contributes two, C–OH one and the bond to the attached group one: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.

questions.prompt: What does a structural formula show that a molecular formula alone may not?
questions.explanation: A molecular formula counts atoms; a structural formula adds connectivity.

questions.prompt: Why is ethanoic acid not classified as an alcohol just because it contains OH?
options: Its OH belongs to a complete –COOH group on a carbonyl carbon.
OH is never bonded to hydrogen.
questions.explanation: Read C=O and O–H together on the same carbon.

questions.prompt: An acid formula is redrawn with C=O tilted upward and OH downward. What has changed?
options: A new atom has been created.
The display of the same connectivity, not the identity of the compound.
The acid has necessarily become an alcohol.
questions.explanation: The drawing directions help reading; rotating a drawing does not change which atoms are bonded.

questions.prompt: What is the systematic name of CH₃OH?
questions.explanation: One carbon gives meth-, and the alcohol group gives –ol.

questions.prompt: Name CH₃–CH₂–OH.
questions.explanation: Two carbons give eth-; the alcohol ending is –ol.

questions.prompt: Name CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–OH using the lowest OH position.
questions.explanation: Number from the OH end: three carbons, OH at carbon 1.

questions.prompt: Name CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₃.
questions.explanation: The three-carbon chain has OH on its middle carbon, carbon 2.

questions.prompt: What is the preferred name for CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–OH in this lesson?
questions.explanation: There are four carbons; numbering from OH gives the lowest locant, 1.

questions.prompt: What is the systematic name of H–C(=O)–OH?
questions.explanation: The carboxyl carbon is the only carbon: methanoic acid.

questions.prompt: Name CH₃COOH, remembering the carboxyl carbon.
questions.explanation: Count the CH₃ carbon and the COOH carbon: two.

questions.prompt: Name CH₃–CH₂–COOH.
questions.explanation: There are three carbons including the carboxyl carbon.

questions.prompt: What is the systematic name of CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–COOH?
questions.explanation: Four carbon atoms give but-, followed by the carboxylic-acid ending –oic acid.

questions.prompt: Which statement about acetic acid is correct?
options: It is another name for ethanol.
It is the systematic name of a four-carbon acid.
It is a common name for ethanoic acid.
questions.explanation: Ethanoic acid and acetic acid name the same compound. Sodium ethanoate is a salt, not unchanged ethanoic acid.

questions.prompt: What is a solvent?
options: A substance that dissolves another substance.
A gas that must turn limewater milky.
questions.explanation: Ethanol can act as a solvent in formulated products.

questions.prompt: What do the short-chain alcohols here share despite different chain lengths?
options: Exactly the same total carbon count.
A carboxyl group in every molecule.
questions.explanation: Methanol, ethanol and propan-1-ol have different carbon counts but share the alcohol pattern.

questions.prompt: In the ordinary dilute-water comparison, how is ethanol described?
questions.explanation: Its bonded OH is not a free hydroxide ion, and ethanol is approximately neutral in this comparison.

questions.prompt: Which products form in the simplified yeast fermentation of glucose?
questions.explanation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.

questions.prompt: What is the role of yeast enzymes in the fermentation model?
options: They supply new carbon atoms from nothing.
They are position numbers in an alcohol name.
questions.explanation: An enzyme is a biological catalyst that speeds the reaction without being consumed overall.

questions.prompt: Which condition belongs to the simplified yeast fermentation described in the book?
options: A guarantee that ethanoic acid is the only product.
The same process as neutralising vinegar with NaOH.
questions.explanation: Keep oxygen-poor fermentation distinct from ethanol oxidation in vinegar production.

questions.prompt: In 2C₂H₅OH, what does the coefficient 2 multiply?
questions.explanation: A coefficient counts complete molecules; it does not change the formula inside each molecule.

questions.prompt: How many carbon atoms are in two ethanol molecules?
questions.explanation: Each ethanol contains two carbons, so 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the water-solubility trend taught for these alcohols?
options: A longer carbon chain generally reduces water solubility, even when OH remains.
Adding a carbon always removes the OH group.
Solubility means the number of bonds on carbon.
questions.explanation: The carbon-containing part becomes larger while the hydroxyl group is still present.

questions.prompt: Why does the name “alcohol” not guarantee that a substance is suitable for drinking?
options: It means all alcohols are dilute acids.
It is a chemical family name; different members have different properties and hazards.
It means every member is ethanol.
It means a molecule contains no carbon.
questions.explanation: Methanol and ethanol are different compounds; the book uses family names to describe chemistry.

questions.prompt: What does “aqueous” mean?
questions.explanation: Vinegar is an aqueous solution containing ethanoic acid.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that ethanoic acid is weak in water?
options: There must be very little acid per litre.
All its molecules are sodium ions.
Only a proportion of its molecules ionise.
questions.explanation: Weak describes partial ionisation; dilute describes concentration.

questions.prompt: What does “dilute” describe?
options: A molecule with only one bond.
questions.explanation: Concentration concerns amount per stated amount or volume of solution.

questions.prompt: Which question is about acid strength rather than concentration?
options: How much acid is present per solution volume?
How extensively does the acid ionise under the stated conditions?
How much solution is in the bottle?
questions.explanation: Strength concerns ionisation; amount per solution volume concerns concentration.

questions.prompt: In CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺, which species is the ethanoate ion?
questions.explanation: The acid has donated H⁺, leaving the negatively charged ethanoate ion.

questions.prompt: What does the raised minus sign in CH₃COO⁻ indicate?
options: A fourth type of oxygen atom.
An electrical charge on the ion.
questions.explanation: An ion is an atom or group with an electrical charge.

questions.prompt: How should H⁺ in an aqueous acid equation be understood?
options: As convenient shorthand for a proton associated with water molecules.
As a bare proton permanently isolated from all water.
As the symbol for carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: H⁺ is hydrated in water; the simplified equation omits that detail.

questions.prompt: At about 25 °C, which pH is neutral for water?
questions.explanation: The book uses pH 7 as neutral for water at about 25 °C.

questions.prompt: Can the word “weak” alone give the exact pH of an ethanoic-acid solution?
options: Yes; weak means no ions exist.
No; concentration and the solution conditions also matter.
Yes; every weak acid solution is exactly pH 7.
questions.explanation: Weak does not specify a unique concentration or pH.

questions.prompt: Why is “all weak acid solutions have one fixed percentage ionised” unreliable?
options: Weak acids have no functional group.
The carboxyl carbon disappears in water.
The extent of ionisation can also depend on concentration and conditions.
questions.explanation: Weak is a description of acid behaviour; it is not one fixed ionisation percentage for every solution.

questions.prompt: What products form when ethanoic acid neutralises sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O.

questions.prompt: What is a salt in the ionic-compound sense used here?
options: A position number in a name.
A compound made from positive and negative ions.
questions.explanation: Sodium ethanoate contains sodium ions and ethanoate ions.

questions.prompt: Does the word neutralisation guarantee that any chosen mixture finishes at pH 7?
options: No, because neutralisation cannot make water.
No; the final solution depends on substances and amounts mixed.
questions.explanation: Neutralisation names the reaction, not a universal final-pH guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which gas is expected from vinegar reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate?
questions.explanation: The acid–hydrogencarbonate reaction gives a salt, water and CO₂.

questions.prompt: What is another familiar name for sodium hydrogencarbonate?
questions.explanation: Sodium hydrogencarbonate is NaHCO₃, commonly called baking soda.

questions.prompt: What is effervescence?
options: A guarantee that the liquid is boiling.
The dissolution of all carbon atoms.
questions.explanation: Effervescence is gas formation; bubbles alone do not identify the gas.

questions.prompt: Which standard observation supports identifying the gas as carbon dioxide?
options: Its presence always makes ethanol strongly basic.
It removes the carboxyl carbon from every remaining acid molecule.
It must have a blue colour.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky in the standard gas test.

questions.prompt: In the ordinary comparison, should ethanol show the same acid–carbonate effervescence as ethanoic acid?
options: Yes, because both contain the letters OH.
No, because ethanol has no oxygen.
No; their complete functional groups have different behaviour.
questions.explanation: A bonded alcohol OH is not the same as the OH in a carboxyl group.

questions.prompt: Which set lists all the products in CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → … ?
questions.explanation: The salt, water and CO₂ account for the atoms supplied by the acid and hydrogencarbonate.

questions.prompt: Why is observing bubbles alone insufficient to identify a gas?
options: Every bubbling process is the same chemical reaction.
Different gases can form bubbles, so an appropriate identification test is needed.
Bubbles can only ever contain hydrogen.
questions.explanation: Distinguish the observation, gas formation, from the interpretation, the gas identity.

questions.category: Ethanol oxidation and comparing the families
questions.prompt: Which organic product forms in the simplified oxidation of ethanol followed in this class?
questions.explanation: CH₃CH₂OH + O₂ → CH₃COOH + H₂O.

questions.category: Ethanol oxidation and comparing the families
questions.prompt: What happens to the two-carbon skeleton in the ethanol-to-ethanoic-acid conversion?
options: It necessarily becomes a one-carbon skeleton.
It gains four new carbon atoms from oxygen.
It remains two carbons long while the end group changes.
questions.explanation: The alcohol end becomes a carboxyl group; the two carbons are retained.

questions.category: Ethanol oxidation and comparing the families
questions.prompt: In the oxidation description used for this conversion, what can oxidation mean?
options: Adding a position number to a name.
questions.explanation: The book uses this introductory description for the ethanol conversion.

questions.category: Ethanol oxidation and comparing the families
questions.prompt: Which process uses glucose to produce ethanol and CO₂ under the stated oxygen-poor conditions?
questions.explanation: Do not confuse the different starting substances and conditions.

questions.category: Ethanol oxidation and comparing the families
questions.prompt: Which comparison between fermentation and vinegar production is correct?
options: Both are identical to reacting vinegar with baking soda.
Fermentation makes ethanol from glucose; the vinegar conversion uses oxygen to oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid.
Both always have ethanoic acid as their only product.
questions.explanation: Follow the starting molecule and reaction conditions rather than just noticing bubbles.

questions.category: Ethanol oxidation and comparing the families
questions.prompt: What does the ordinary reversible arrow ⇌ indicate?
options: The amounts on both sides must be equal.
Carbon atoms do not need to be conserved.
The reaction can proceed in both directions.
questions.explanation: The arrow describes possible reaction directions; it is not a statement of equal amounts.

questions.category: Ethanol oxidation and comparing the families
questions.prompt: Which statement is a sensible limit of the ethanol example?
options: Do not assume every alcohol oxidises to the same acid.
Every alcohol must give ethanoic acid.
No alcohol can change functional group.
questions.explanation: The class follows a particular primary-alcohol conversion, not every possible alcohol reaction.

questions.category: Ethanol oxidation and comparing the families
questions.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are present on the reactant side of CH₃CH₂OH + O₂ → CH₃COOH + H₂O?
questions.explanation: One O is in ethanol and two are in O₂: three in total.

questions.category: Ethanol oxidation and comparing the families
questions.prompt: Which evidence-and-reasoning sequence is most appropriate before using the work mat?
options: Choose a family from bottle colour alone.
Ignore the carbonyl and count only loose hydrogens.
Read the complete group, identify the family, predict behaviour, then compare observations.
Call any OH-containing substance an alcohol immediately.
questions.explanation: The lesson builds structure → family → prediction → evidence → explanation.

questions.category: Ethanol oxidation and comparing the families
questions.prompt: A formula has OH attached to a carbon that is also double-bonded to O. What is the best classification?
options: An alcohol simply because OH is visible.
A carboxylic acid with the complete –COOH group.
questions.explanation: The entire carboxyl arrangement, not OH in isolation, determines this classification.
